title: Philemon
hook: a short note asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
carry: no longer a servant, but a brother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the epistle: Paul's letters as real mail, with a scribe's hello and a list of friends. Your line was names matter. Whose name went into your card? Day eighty-eight.

Have you ever had to write a note on someone else's behalf? A reference. A text to smooth things over between two friends. You choose every word, because someone's future is riding on it. Paul's shortest letter is exactly that. It fits on a single page. It's written from prison to a man named Philemon, a believer with a church meeting in his home. And it's about a young man named Onesimus. Onesimus is enslaved in Philemon's household, and he has left it. Somewhere along the way he found Paul, in prison, and became a believer. Now Paul is sending him back, carrying this letter. Philemon has the law on his side, and the power to punish. Everything depends on the words on this page.
screen: `A NOTE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `ONE PAGE, FROM PRISON.` → `ONESIMUS GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Listen to how Paul does it. He says he could order Philemon to do the right thing, but he'd rather appeal, for love's sake. He calls Onesimus my son, my very heart. And he makes a joke, because the name Onesimus means useful: "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me." Then he says what he's really asking. Take him back, the King James Bible says, "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved." The word the old English translates as servant is doulos, which means slave. Paul is asking a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother, in the flesh, as well as in the Lord. Then he signs a blank check: "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account." I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it. And he ends, knowing you'll do even more than I say. Now the honest part. The letter never says, in so many words, set him free, and it doesn't tell us why Onesimus left, or what Philemon did next. The Bible is silent. Over the centuries, some Christians used Paul's letters to defend slavery, and others, including many who fought to end it, read this page as pointing the other way: once a man is your brother, how can he be your property? A few decades later, a bishop of Ephesus was named Onesimus. Some have wondered if it was the same man. Nobody knows. What we have is one page, where Paul puts his own name on the line for someone with less power, and asks for a new word: brother.
screen: `FOR LOVE'S SAKE, NOT ORDERS.` · `ONESIMUS MEANS USEFUL.` · `PUT THAT ON MINE ACCOUNT.` · `THE BIBLE IS SILENT ON WHAT CAME NEXT.` · then, large: `A BROTHER BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for someone with less power. Sit, and breathe. Think of someone in your world who has less say than the people around them. A new employee. A kid. Someone who cleans the office after everyone leaves. Someone whose English is still new. Is there a word you could put in for them, the way Paul did? A thank you said where the boss can hear. A good reference. Putting something on your account. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Philemon. Paul's shortest letter, asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother.
Your line: no longer a servant, but a brother. Today, put in one good word for someone with less power, where it counts. Tomorrow, a letter to a quarreling church. Day eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Philemon is read in churches as a letter about reconciliation and about how faith changes relationships of power. It was also central in debates over slavery, when abolitionists and defenders of slavery read it in opposite ways.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in prison. Onesimus has to go back to Philemon, who has every legal right to punish him. what do you write?
options: an order: free him at once.
an appeal: receive him as a brother, and charge any debt to me.
nothing. it's between the two of them.
fork.reveal: Paul appeals for love's sake: not now as a servant, but a brother beloved. if he owes thee anything, put that on mine account.

original.note: Greek: useful, profitable. A common name for enslaved people, and the root of Paul's pun.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short, forgettable page between longer letters.
what it means: Paul puts his own name and money on the line to ask a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother.
what a scholar hears: doulos means slave, Onesimus means useful, the outcome is unknown, and the letter was read in opposite ways in the slavery debates.

notes: Why Onesimus left is debated (runaway; sent on an errand; seeking Paul as a mediator). The script says only that he 'has left' and that the letter doesn't tell us why.
History of use in slavery debates, stated briefly and without drama; confirm tone.
Ignatius's letter to the Ephesians (early 2nd century) names a bishop Onesimus; identification with Philemon's Onesimus is speculative, and the script says nobody knows.
'In the flesh, as well as in the Lord' paraphrases Philemon 1:16b ('both in the flesh, and in the Lord'). Confirm.
The index carry 'no longer a servant, but a brother' paraphrases 1:16; kept exactly as the index gives it.
